scenario.name: Splunk STRT, Mandiant & CISA — Citrix Bleed: NetScaler OOB Memory Leak & NSC_AAAC Hijack
scenario.shortSubtitle: Splunk STRT / Mandiant / CISA AA23-325A · CVE-2023-4966 Host Header Leak, NSC_AAAC Cookie & VDI Pivot
scenario.overview: Picture a wide multi-lane city highway approaching an overhead exit sign gantry and a row of striped toll plaza booths with automated lifting barrier arms. Cruising down the multi-lane express highway, a driver mounts a cloned electronic toll transponder behind the windshield right before entering the fast-pass lane. In this real-world scenario, the intruder steps up to the overhead license-plate gantry blending in with everyday guests, then completes the covert maneuver at the express highway toll barrier while the highway toll camera log records the anomaly. The highway authority’s overhead license-plate camera spots two different vehicles using the same toll pass minutes apart and sounds an immediate toll-plaza alert. In this scenario (CVE-2023-4966, Splunk STRT, Mandiant & CISA, Citrix Bleed: NetScaler OOB Memory Leak & NSC_AAAC Hijack), the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: sending an Oversized HTTP "Host" Header, then extracting the 65-Character "NSC_AAAC", then pivoting from the Hijacked Citrix VDI. Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering Sending an Oversized HTTP "Host" Header, then Extracting the 65-Character "NSC_AAAC", then Pivoting from the Hijacked Citrix VDI, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible so you can see which trusted process launched the next payload. Primary detection correlates Sysmon Event 1 with the documented host and network chain.

stages.title: NETSCALER SNPRINTF OOB MEMORY LEAK (CVE-2023-4966)
stages.subtitle: Sending 24KB Host header to /oauth/idp/.well-known/openid-configuration
stages.description: Cruising down the multi-lane express highway, a driver mounts a cloned electronic toll transponder behind the windshield right before entering the fast-pass lane. Specifically in Step 1, the intruder steps up to the overhead license-plate gantry blending in with everyday guests while everyday visitors and the toll booth attendant go about their routine. As reverse-engineered by Assetnote, the attacker sends an unauthenticated HTTPS GET request to /oauth/idp/.well-known/openid-configuration (a public discovery page on the Citrix NetScaler Gateway whose ns_aaa_oauthrp_send_openid_config function inserts the caller’s HTTP Host header into six JSON URL fields: issuer, authorization_endpoint, token_endpoint, jwks_uri, userinfo_endpoint, and end_session_endpoint). By sending a 24,576-byte Host header, the 6 copies total ~147 KB, exceeding the server’s 131,072-byte (0x20000) stack response buffer. Because C’s snprintf() function returns how many bytes it wanted to write (147 KB) rather than how many bytes actually fit in the 128 KB buffer, NetScaler’s SSL_write transmits the 128 KB buffer PLUS ~16 KB of raw adjacent nsppe memory straight back to the attacker. In the C standard library, snprintf(buf, size, fmt...) stops writing at size bytes to prevent a crash, but returns the theoretical total length of the formatted string. Passing that unchecked return value directly to the HTTP socket writer causes an out-of-bounds memory over-read (CVE-2023-4966) from the NetScaler packet engine (nsppe). In the documented Suricata CVE-2023-4966 exchange from Threat Actor (LockBit / UNC) to DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap, DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap responds with ALERT 148 KB Leak (confirming that the CITRIX BLEED GET request succeeded on DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 NSC_AAAC SESSION COOKIE EXTRACTION & MFA BYPASS). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ CITRIX BLEED GET / ⇠#1 ALERT 148 KB Leak) from Node ① (#1 Threat Actor (LockBit / UNC)) to Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Splunk Enterprise Security (STRT)).

stages.title: NSC_AAAC SESSION COOKIE EXTRACTION & MFA BYPASS
stages.subtitle: Carving 65-byte hex NSC_AAAC token from leaked memory and replaying
stages.description: As the car rolls beneath the overhead highway gantry, the toll booth reader recognizes the cloned pass signal and automatically lifts the striped barrier arm. Here in Step 2 inside the highway toll plaza, the intruder quietly copies a trusted access pass from the toll booth attendant's station without disturbing the local side-road ramp. Scanning the leaked raw memory dump with a regular expression ([0-9a-f]{32,65}), the attacker extracts a 65-character hexadecimal string: a live NSC_AAAC session cookie (the master authentication token stored in nsppe memory for a user who has already logged in and passed Multi-Factor Authentication). By pasting Cookie: NSC_AAAC=<leaked_token> into their own browser, the attacker hijacks the administrator’s active Citrix session (bypassing both the password screen and MFA completely). Because the NSC_AAAC cookie represents an active server-side AAA session in NetScaler memory, even patching the appliance or resetting the victim’s Active Directory password does not kick the attacker out unless the administrator explicitly flushes active sessions on the appliance via kill aaa session -all and kill icaconnection -all. In the documented NetScaler SSLVPN Log exchange from DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap to Citrix NetScaler ADC / Gateway, Citrix NetScaler ADC / Gateway responds with RESP IP Mismatch (confirming that the REPLAY NSC_AAAC request succeeded on Citrix NetScaler ADC / Gateway and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 CITRIX ICA VDI LAUNCH & INTERNAL AD RECONNAISSANCE). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ REPLAY NSC_AAAC / ⇠#2 RESP IP Mismatch) from Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Citrix NetScaler ADC / Gateway), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Splunk Enterprise Security (STRT)).

stages.title: CITRIX ICA VDI LAUNCH & INTERNAL AD RECONNAISSANCE
stages.subtitle: Downloading launch.ica to pivot onto internal VDI workstation
stages.description: The vehicle accelerates smoothly through the express toll lane onto the restricted city bypass while every ordinary commuter waits in the cash queue next door. In this final step inside the highway toll plaza, the intruder completes the covert maneuver at the express highway toll barrier while the highway toll camera log records the anomaly until the highway toll camera log catches the mismatch. Inside the hijacked Citrix Virtual Desktop (VDI) session, the attacker runs Active Directory discovery tools (adfind / SoftPerfect netscan), deploys remote management tunnels (AnyDesk / eHorus), and uses Distributed COM (DCOM, invoking the MMC20.Application COM object over RPC port 135, which instructs a remote Windows server to silently launch mmc.exe -Embedding and execute commands via Document.ActiveView.ExecuteShellCommand without creating a noisy new Windows service). Unlike PsExec or sc.exe (which register a new Windows Service and trigger System EventID 7045 on the target server), lateral movement via DCOM MMC20.Application abuses an already-registered Microsoft COM class over TCP/135. Mechanically, this stage is complete only after [object Object] and [object Object] is observed as live runtime state (the concrete checkpoint proving the previous stage's output now drives the next action). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ VDI POWERSHELL RECON / ⇠#3 ACK PID 5310) from Node ③ (#3 Citrix NetScaler ADC / Gateway) to Node ④ (#4 Hijacked NSC_AAAC Session), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Splunk Enterprise Security (STRT)).

detectionRule.title: Splunk STRT / CISA — Citrix Bleed CVE-2023-4966 Memory Leak Response
detectionRule.ruleCode: alert http any any -> $HOME_NET any (msg:"CISA AA23-325A Citrix Bleed CVE-2023-4966 Oversized Host Header"; flow:established,to_server; http.uri; content:"/oauth/idp/.well-known/openid-configuration"; http.host; bsize:>4096; classtype:attempted-recon; sid:20234966; rev:1;)
detectionRule.mitigation: Patch Citrix NetScaler ADC/Gateway AND run "kill icaconnection -all" and "kill rdp connection -all" followed by "clear ns partition" to invalidate leaked NSC_AAAC tokens.

detectionRule.title: Citrix NetScaler Session Hijack (Multiple Client IPs per SessionId)
detectionRule.ruleCode:
title: Citrix NetScaler SSLVPN Session Used From Multiple Client IPs
logsource:
  product: citrix
  service: netscaler
detection:
  selection:
    EventType: 'TCPCONNSTAT'
  condition: selection
level: critical
detectionRule.mitigation: Correlate NetScaler SessionId values in /var/log/ns.log and terminate any session where Client_ip differs from the initial authentication Context IP.

detectionRule.title: Citrix VDI Shell (wfshell.exe) Spawning Hidden PowerShell or Recon Tools
detectionRule.ruleCode:
title: Suspicious Child Process of Citrix wfshell.exe
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith: '\wfshell.exe'
    Image|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\net.exe'
      - '\AnyDesk.exe'
  condition: selection
level: high
detectionRule.mitigation: Enforce PowerShell Constrained Language Mode and AppLocker policies on Citrix VDI images.
